documents.title: Reference data set documentation – mortgage acceptance scorecard v3.0

sections.heading: Purpose and scope
sections.text: This document describes the construction, content, representativeness and data quality of the reference data set (RDS) for version 3.0 of the Mortgage Acceptance Scorecard (MAS v3.0, model inventory identifier MDL-18). It follows the RDS documentation template of MRM-STD-021 Annex A and is version-controlled in the controlled document repository. Cover block: document title "Reference data set documentation – Mortgage Acceptance Scorecard v3.0"; model MDL-18, model version 3.0; document version 0.6; status Draft; author L. Mulder (Senior Model Developer, Retail Credit Risk Modelling); reviewer K. de Vries (Model Developer, Retail Credit Risk Modelling); approver E. Visser (Director Retail Credit Risk, Model Owner); approval date pending. MAS v3.0 is an internally developed application scorecard used, together with policy rules, the affordability assessment and the collateral assessment, to recommend accept, refer or decline for new Dutch residential mortgage applications of natural persons; it is managed as a model under MRM-POL-001. The scope of application comprises all new mortgage applications for owner-occupied residential property in the Netherlands submitted through intermediaries or the Bank's own advisers, including applications with a Nationale Hypotheek Garantie (NHG). Further advances on existing mortgages, buy-to-let lending and bridge loans are out of scope.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all mortgage applications received between 1 January 2019 and 30 September 2024 (through-the-door population, one record per application at the date of the final underwriting decision): 356,200 applications with 548,300 applicants. Of these, 251,900 were accepted (70.7%), 62,300 declined (17.5%) and 42,000 withdrawn or not completed (11.8%); 210,400 accepted applications resulted in a disbursed loan. Performance is observed monthly up to 31 March 2027; within the 24-month performance window there are 926 bad outcomes (0.44% of disbursed loans), 2,314 indeterminate outcomes and 207,160 good outcomes.

sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The development sample is drawn from the most recent through-the-door population for which the 24-month performance window is complete: applications up to 30 September 2024, with disbursement up to 31 March 2025 and outcomes to 31 March 2027. The start in January 2019 follows the introduction of the current application processing platform (HAP) in December 2018, from which structured application and verification data are available for all channels. The window covers a period of low interest rates (2019–2021), the pandemic with payment holidays for 1,140 borrowers in 2020, and the rise of mortgage rates from 1.8% to 4.3% between 2022 and 2023 together with high inflation. It therefore includes both benign and stressed conditions for affordability, although no period of house price decline with rising unemployment comparable to 2011–2013 is included (limitation LIM-18-02).

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target is a bad flag: the loan becomes 90 or more days past due or is in default under CR-STD-110 at any time within 24 months after disbursement. Loans reaching a maximum delinquency of 30–89 days past due without becoming bad are indeterminate (2,314 loans, 1.1%) and are excluded from estimation but included in the score distribution analyses; all other disbursed loans are good. The target is assumed to measure the applicant's inability to meet the obligations of the credit agreement in the early years of the loan, and the application data are assumed to represent the applicant's verified situation at the time of the decision. The 24-month window follows CR-STD-120 §5.1 for mortgages and is supported by the maturity analysis in Annex B: 71% of bads within 48 months occur within the first 24 months.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: The bad flag deviates from the CR-STD-110 default definition in one respect: 90 days past due is counted without the materiality threshold (EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative), because in the first two years of a mortgage any 90-day arrear is a strong signal of affordability problems. The deviation adds 23 bad outcomes (2.5% of bads) to the 903 default events; 19 of these loans were cured after a payment arrangement and four defaulted after the window. Estimating the scorecard with the strict default flag changes the out-of-time Gini by −0.3 percentage points and does not change the ranking of the characteristics. The deviation was approved by the Model Owner as expert judgement EJ-18-01.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The default flag is taken from the default register maintained under CR-STD-110 and is applied at obligor level: all applicants of a mortgage are one obligor and a default of any borrower in the household defaults the loan. The flag uses 90 days past due above the materiality threshold of EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative, unlikeliness to pay, a probation period of three months (twelve months for distressed restructuring) and multiple default handling as specified in CR-STD-110. For the period January 2019 to December 2020, before the Bank implemented the EBA definition of default on 1 January 2021, the default flag is approximated by reconstructing the materiality threshold and the probation period from daily arrears data; the approximation affects 212 loans and changes the number of defaults by +4.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers are applied at obligor level and sourced from the arrears management system (AMS) and the default register: distressed restructuring (forbearance with a diminished financial obligation above 1%), forced sale of the collateral, debt restructuring under the Wet schuldsanering natuurlijke personen (WSNP), a claim on the NHG guarantee, specific credit risk adjustment, and bankruptcy of the borrower. Within the 24-month window, 61 of the 926 bad outcomes were triggered by unlikeliness to pay without reaching 90 days past due.

sections.heading: Data sources and lineage
sections.text: The RDS is sourced from six data domains, each with one Data Owner recorded in the Group Data Catalogue: Mortgage Origination (application processing platform HAP), Mortgage Servicing (mortgage administration system HAS and arrears management system AMS), Credit Risk (default register), Collateral (collateral management system CMS), Customer (customer master CIF) and External Credit Data (BKR bureau reports). Lineage from source system to RDS field is documented in Annex A for every variable, including discarded variables used to construct retained characteristics. Per variable the lineage identifies the source system and fields, the intermediate stores (credit risk data warehouse staging and integration layers), each transformation, filter, join and aggregation with the performing SAS job or dbt model, and the extraction frequency and timing. The application data were collected from applicants and intermediaries for the purpose of assessing their mortgage application and creditworthiness; their use for developing the acceptance model is documented together with this original purpose. Information on income, expenses and other financial circumstances is obtained from the applicant and the intermediary, from internal sources (current account data of existing customers) and from external sources (BKR, employer statements, UWV employment history and tax documents).

sections.heading: Application and verification data
sections.text: The RDS records, for every application, the information used in the creditworthiness assessment: loan purpose, employment and employment type, gross income and income source per applicant, household composition and dependants, existing financial commitments (BKR registrations, student loans, alimony, ground lease), regular expenses used in the affordability calculation, the collateral and other risk mitigants such as NHG. Income is verified with independent documents: an employer's statement and recent salary slip, the UWV employment history statement (UWV Verzekeringsbericht) and, for self-employed applicants, an income statement by an accredited party (Inkomensverklaring Ondernemer) based on three years of tax returns. Where information is inconsistent (for example employer name or income differing between documents), the underwriter makes further enquiries with the applicant or the employer; these checks are recorded in HAP as verification events and are available in the RDS. The information requested from applicants is specified in the Bank's document checklist provided to intermediaries in the pre-contractual phase and is limited to what the creditworthiness assessment requires. HAP stores the credit-granting criteria actually applied to each application (policy rule results, score, affordability outcome, LTV) together with every policy deviation, exception and override with reason code; these fields are part of the RDS.

sections.heading: Credit bureau and other external data
sections.text: For BKR bureau data the lineage starts at the receipt of the bureau report in HAP and records the provider (Stichting BKR), the data product (the BKR credit check with registration details and arrears codes) and the retrieval timestamp of each report. The Bank consults BKR as a participant under the BKR general regulations, which provide access to all participating lenders under the same conditions, and uses the data only for the creditworthiness assessment of the application and for monitoring the borrower's compliance with credit obligations. Applicants are informed in the application form and by their intermediary, before the check, that BKR will be consulted. All data are processed in the Netherlands; no personal data used in the RDS are transferred outside the EEA. For the reject inference check (section 4.4), BKR data on credit obtained elsewhere by declined applicants were retrieved for the permitted purpose of credit risk model development under the BKR regulations.

sections.heading: Collateral and valuation data
sections.text: Collateral data (property type, market value, valuation date and method, lien rank and link to the secured loan) are taken from the collateral management system CMS and are subject to the data quality rules of this RDS. Every valuation used at origination is a full valuation report by a valuer registered with the Nederlands Register Vastgoed Taxateurs (NRVT), validated by the Nederlands Woning Waarde Instituut (NWWI) and stored in CMS as a PDF in durable form with its validation certificate. Valuers are assigned through the NWWI platform independently of the intermediary and the underwriter, and the Bank's valuation policy excludes valuers with a link to the transaction. For 4,120 NHG applications in 2023–2024 with a purchase price below the NHG limit, a model-based valuation (desktop valuation) was accepted under the NHG conditions; these are identified by a valuation method code.

sections.heading: Manual interventions and lineage changes
sections.text: The RDS build contains no manual data manipulation. The only manual input is the mapping of 312 free-text employer sectors to 14 sector groups, held as a version-controlled file (sector_map_v2.csv) and documented as expert judgement EJ-18-02. The build is fully automated through scheduled jobs; the sector mapping file is the only manual element and is controlled through four-eyes review. Changes to the definition, source or transformation of a critical data element require approval by the Data Owner and advance notification to the Model Owner. The lineage was updated before use after the migration of arrears data from AMS v4 to AMS v5 in June 2022, and the continuity of days-past-due counting across the migration was verified.

sections.heading: Exclusions
sections.text: Four exclusions are applied. (1) Applications by staff under staff mortgage conditions: 3,960 applications (1.1%), 5 bads. (2) Applications for properties under construction with the valuation on completion only (new-build without land registry valuation at decision): 6,210 applications (1.7%), 9 bads. (3) Duplicate applications resubmitted by a different intermediary within 30 days (the latest submission is retained): 8,740 applications (2.5%). (4) Loans taken over within 24 months by another lender after sale of the property without arrears (performance truncated): 2,880 loans (1.4% of disbursed), 0 bads. Each exclusion is justified, quantified and assessed for its effect on representativeness in section 5.3. No exclusion exceeds 5% of records or exposure in any segment; the exclusions were nevertheless approved by the Model Owner on 16 April 2027 and reported to Model Validation.

sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in Annex C, distinguishing structural missing values (for example months in current employment for pensioners and self-employed applicants, no BKR history for applicants without credit), values missing at random (1.3% of applications without a recorded own-funds amount) and values missing because of a data deficiency (verification timestamps before March 2020, DD-18-02). Structural missing values form a separate attribute class in the coarse classing; values missing at random are assigned to the attribute class with the closest bad rate, a documented and reproducible rule, and the share of such values per variable and the effect on the estimated points (at most 2 points) are reported in Annex C. Outliers are identified with documented criteria (values outside the 0.1st and 99.9th percentile or outside business-valid ranges, such as LTV above 106%) and are floored or capped at those values; the same rules are part of the implementation specification, so that development and production treatment is identical, and their impact on the score is below 1 point for 99% of applications. The bad flag is never imputed: 37 loans with inconsistent arrears data were investigated and corrected at source in AMS.

sections.heading: Declined applications and reject inference data
sections.text: The known good/bad sample contains only accepted and disbursed applications, so the RDS also contains the 62,300 declined applications with their application characteristics and decline reasons, as input for reject inference: 41,900 were declined by statutory affordability limits or policy rules, 13,700 by the current scorecard cut-off and 6,700 by underwriters (high-side overrides). For 11,300 declined applicants, BKR data 24 months after the decline show new consumer credit obtained elsewhere; their bureau outcome (a BKR arrears code within 24 months) is stored as the external performance used to calibrate and check the inferred bad rates, as documented in MDD section 4.4. The 42,000 withdrawn applications are not used for reject inference, because the withdrawal decision was the applicant's; their score distribution is comparable to accepted applications (PSI 0.04).

sections.heading: Representativeness
sections.text: Representativeness of the development sample for the current applicant population was tested with the PSI of each characteristic and of the score of the current model (MAS v2.1) between the development sample and the applications of October 2025 to March 2026: the score PSI is 0.08 and the characteristic PSIs range from 0.01 to 0.14; LTV band (0.14) and interest fixation period (0.12) are amber against the 0.10 threshold and no characteristic is red. The amber shifts reflect higher LTVs of starters after the abolition of transfer tax for starters and a shift towards 10- and 20-year fixation after the rate rise; both segments are well populated in the development sample (19,800 and 64,300 applications), so the data remain relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose. The statistical properties of the data were checked for the groups of persons on whom the system will be used: applicants by age band, household type, employment type and income band are all represented with at least 2,000 applications and 30 bads per group except self-employed applicants (6,900 applications, 21 bads), which is recorded as limitation LIM-18-04. Detailed tables are in Annex B.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Staff applications have a lower bad rate (0.13%) and more favourable characteristics, and are processed under separate staff conditions in production. New-build applications without a valuation at decision are scored in production after the valuation on completion is available, so their exclusion does not affect the scored population; their characteristics are comparable (PSI 0.05). Duplicate submissions would double-count applicants. Loans taken over within 24 months without arrears would bias the bad rate downwards if treated as good; including them as good changes the bad rate from 0.440% to 0.434%. The combined exclusions change the development bad rate by less than 0.01 percentage points and the characteristic distributions by at most PSI 0.02. The exclusions are therefore not expected to affect representativeness.

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development against the mandatory dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness of MRM-STD-022, supplemented by validity, uniqueness and appropriateness. Completeness was measured at record level (all applications in HAP and all disbursed loans in HAS included, and all defaults in the default register linked) and at attribute level. Consistency was assessed between the RDS and the production input data of the decision engine (replay of 5,000 applications from March 2027: 99.8% of characteristic values identical), across the observation period including the change in default definition in 2021, and through logical rules between related fields. Timeliness was measured as the lag between the decision date and data availability and as the age of the valuation and of the BKR report at the decision date (valuation at most six months, BKR report at most one month old). Because MAS is a Tier 1 model, the assessment included a sample-based verification of 600 applications against the credit files (income documents, employer statements, BKR reports and valuation reports). The detailed results per rule, variable and dimension and the number and share of excluded records per reason are reported in EVD-18-DQR. The assessment concluded that the data are fit for the intended use and was signed off by the developer and the Model Owner on 16 April 2027, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Observation period
sections.text: The RDS covers all mortgage applications received between 1 January 2019 and 30 September 2024 (through-the-door population, one record per application at the date of the final underwriting decision): 356,200 applications with 548,300 applicants. sections.heading: Choice of observation window
sections.text: The development sample is drawn from the most recent through-the-door population for which the 24-month performance window is complete: applications up to 30 September 2024, with disbursement up to 31 March 2025 and outcomes to 31 March 2027. The start in January 2019 follows the introduction of the current application processing platform (HAP) in December 2018, from which structured application and verification data are available for all channels. The window covers a period of low interest rates (2019–2021), the pandemic with payment holidays for 1,140 borrowers in 2020, and the rise of mortgage rates from 1.8% to 4.3% between 2022 and 2023 together with high inflation. It therefore includes both benign and stressed conditions for affordability, although no period of house price decline with rising unemployment comparable to 2011–2013 is included (limitation LIM-18-02).

sections.heading: Target variable and outcome horizon
sections.text: The target is a bad flag: the loan becomes 90 or more days past due or is in default under CR-STD-110 at any time within 24 months after disbursement. Loans reaching a maximum delinquency of 30–89 days past due without becoming bad are indeterminate (2,314 loans, 1.1%) and are excluded from estimation but included in the score distribution analyses; all other disbursed loans are good. The target is assumed to measure the applicant's inability to meet the obligations of the credit agreement in the early years of the loan, and the application data are assumed to represent the applicant's verified situation at the time of the decision. The 24-month window follows CR-STD-120 §5.1 for mortgages and is supported by the maturity analysis in Annex B: 71% of bads within 48 months occur within the first 24 months.

sections.heading: Deviations from the Bank's definition of default
sections.text: The bad flag deviates from the CR-STD-110 default definition in one respect: 90 days past due is counted without the materiality threshold (EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative), because in the first two years of a mortgage any 90-day arrear is a strong signal of affordability problems. The deviation adds 23 bad outcomes (2.5% of bads) to the 903 default events; 19 of these loans were cured after a payment arrangement and four defaulted after the window. Estimating the scorecard with the strict default flag changes the out-of-time Gini by −0.3 percentage points and does not change the ranking of the characteristics. The deviation was approved by the Model Owner as expert judgement EJ-18-01.

sections.heading: Default definition
sections.text: The default flag is taken from the default register maintained under CR-STD-110 and is applied at obligor level: all applicants of a mortgage are one obligor and a default of any borrower in the household defaults the loan. The flag uses 90 days past due above the materiality threshold of EUR 100 absolute and 1% relative, unlikeliness to pay, a probation period of three months (twelve months for distressed restructuring) and multiple default handling as specified in CR-STD-110. For the period January 2019 to December 2020, before the Bank implemented the EBA definition of default on 1 January 2021, the default flag is approximated by reconstructing the materiality threshold and the probation period from daily arrears data; the approximation affects 212 loans and changes the number of defaults by +4.

sections.heading: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers
sections.text: Unlikeliness-to-pay triggers are applied at obligor level and sourced from the arrears management system (AMS) and the default register: distressed restructuring (forbearance with a diminished financial obligation above 1%), forced sale of the collateral, debt restructuring under the Wet schuldsanering natuurlijke personen (WSNP), a claim on the NHG guarantee, specific credit risk adjustment, and bankruptcy of the borrower. sections.heading: Application and verification data
sections.text: The RDS records, for every application, the information used in the creditworthiness assessment: loan purpose, employment and employment type, gross income and income source per applicant, household composition and dependants, existing financial commitments (BKR registrations, student loans, alimony, ground lease), regular expenses used in the affordability calculation, the collateral and other risk mitigants such as NHG. sections.heading: Missing values and outliers
sections.text: Missing values are treated per variable as documented in Annex C, distinguishing structural missing values (for example months in current employment for pensioners and self-employed applicants, no BKR history for applicants without credit), values missing at random (1.3% of applications without a recorded own-funds amount) and values missing because of a data deficiency (verification timestamps before March 2020, DD-18-02). Structural missing values form a separate attribute class in the coarse classing; values missing at random are assigned to the attribute class with the closest bad rate, a documented and reproducible rule, and the share of such values per variable and the effect on the estimated points (at most 2 points) are reported in Annex C. Outliers are identified with documented criteria (values outside the 0.1st and 99.9th percentile or outside business-valid ranges, such as LTV above 106%) and are floored or capped at those values; the same rules are part of the implementation specification, so that development and production treatment is identical, and their impact on the score is below 1 point for 99% of applications. The bad flag is never imputed: 37 loans with inconsistent arrears data were investigated and corrected at source in AMS.

sections.heading: Impact of exclusions
sections.text: Staff applications have a lower bad rate (0.13%) and more favourable characteristics, and are processed under separate staff conditions in production. sections.heading: Examination of possible biases
sections.text: The training, validation and testing data were examined for possible biases likely to affect fundamental rights or lead to discrimination. Historical decision bias arises because the known outcomes are observed only for applications accepted under the previous scorecard and policy rules, and because underwriter high-side overrides may have excluded applicants on grounds not captured by the data; this feedback loop from past outputs to future training data is the main source of potential bias. Measurement bias affects self-employed income, which is assessed over three years rather than current income. Under-representation affects applicants aged 60 and over (2.9% of applications). Measures taken: reject inference with an external performance check (MDD section 4.4), an analysis of high-side overrides by nationality group, sex and age band (no significant difference in override rates, p = 0.31), exclusion of protected attributes and proxy screening (section 7.3), and disparate outcome testing (MDD section 7.6).

sections.heading: Data quality assessment
sections.text: The data quality of the RDS was assessed before development against the mandatory dimensions completeness, accuracy, consistency and timeliness of MRM-STD-022, supplemented by validity, uniqueness and appropriateness. Completeness was measured at record level (all applications in HAP and all disbursed loans in HAS included, and all defaults in the default register linked) and at attribute level. Consistency was assessed between the RDS and the production input data of the decision engine (replay of 5,000 applications from March 2027: 99.8% of characteristic values identical), across the observation period including the change in default definition in 2021, and through logical rules between related fields. Timeliness was measured as the lag between the decision date and data availability and as the age of the valuation and of the BKR report at the decision date (valuation at most six months, BKR report at most one month old). Because MAS is a Tier 1 model, the assessment included a sample-based verification of 600 applications against the credit files (income documents, employer statements, BKR reports and valuation reports). The detailed results per rule, variable and dimension and the number and share of excluded records per reason are reported in EVD-18-DQR. The assessment concluded that the data are fit for the intended use and was signed off by the developer and the Model Owner on 16 April 2027, before the RDS was frozen.

sections.heading: Data quality rules and thresholds
sections.text: All 13 scorecard characteristics, the 41 candidate characteristics that were constructed from them or considered, and every data element used to construct the bad flag (days past due, default flag and date, disbursement date) are critical data elements. Each of the 86 critical data elements has a business definition, a technical definition and at least one rule per applicable mandatory dimension; where a dimension does not apply, the reason is recorded. The rules are documented in Annex A of EVD-18-DQR and implemented in the Group DQ monitoring tool as rule set DQ-MDL18. sections.heading: Protected attributes and proxy screening
sections.text: Protected attributes (sex, nationality, ethnic origin, religion) are excluded from the scorecard as characteristics, segmentation criteria and override reasons. Age is not a scorecard characteristic; it is used only in the affordability assessment to determine whether the state pension age is reached within ten years, as required by the Trhk, which is legally required and objectively justified by the product; this use was approved by Credit Risk Management on 9 December 2026. No special categories of personal data under Art. 9(1) GDPR are processed; health information that applicants provide in the context of disability income is not captured in the RDS, and automated decisions are therefore not based on special categories. Every candidate characteristic was screened for proxy effects against sex, age band and nationality group (Dutch, other EU, non-EU), combining a qualitative assessment with Cramér's V: months in current employment has a Cramér's V of 0.34 with age band and was retained with a documented credit-risk rationale (job stability), restricted to four coarse classes; postcode was rejected as a characteristic and only province is used in monitoring. The Bank does not process special categories for bias detection; nationality, available from customer due diligence, is used for outcome testing only, so the conditions of Art. 10(5) AI Act do not need to be invoked.

sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: Cover block: document title "Acceptance scorecard development document"; model MDL-18 (Mortgage Acceptance Scorecard), model version 3.0; document version 0.7; status Draft; author L. Mulder; reviewer K. de Vries; approvers E. Visser (Director Retail Credit Risk, Model Owner) and P. Jansen (Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling); approval date pending. MAS v3.0 is a logistic regression application scorecard that ranks new Dutch residential mortgage applications of natural persons by the probability of becoming 90 days past due or defaulted within 24 months, expressed as a score between 480 and 720. Together with the policy rules, the affordability assessment and the collateral assessment it produces an accept, refer or decline recommendation in the mortgage decision engine. The scorecard forms part of the thorough creditworthiness assessment that the Bank performs before concluding every mortgage credit agreement. Intended users are the Bank's mortgage underwriters (acceptants), Retail Credit Risk (cut-off and policy management) and the Retail Credit Committee. The expected bad rate per score band is used as secondary input to risk-based pricing analysis; the score is not used for IRB, provisioning or behavioural purposes. Regulatory use: credit origination. The model is Tier 1. MAS v3.0 will be used in credit decisions only after approval following independent validation, and only within its approved scope of application.

sections.heading: AI system assessment and AI Act classification
sections.text: The scorecard was assessed against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act. Its coefficients and score bands are inferred from historical data by statistical estimation rather than set by humans, and it generates predictions that influence decisions on natural persons; although logistic regression is an established statistical technique, the Bank concluded, conservatively and in agreement with the AI Governance Office (review AIGO-2026-118 of 18 November 2026), that MAS v3.0 qualifies as an AI system. Because it is intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons, MAS v3.0 is classified as a high-risk AI system under Art. 6(2) and Annex III point 5(b) and is registered as such in the model inventory and the AI Inventory (AIUC-2026-041); it is not used for fraud detection. The Art. 6(3) derogation is not relied upon, because the system performs profiling of natural persons. The AI Act classification was recorded in the model inventory before gate G1. The Bank acts as provider (it develops the system and puts it into service under its own name) and as deployer. The high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027; MAS v3.0 is planned to be put into service on 17 January 2028, after the conformity assessment described in the AI Act technical documentation EVD-18-FRIA.

sections.heading: Model design and decision framework
sections.text: Each acceptance decision combines four components, all of which must be passed unless an authorised override applies: (1) policy rules (for example an active BKR default registration, an application fraud indicator, ineligible property type); (2) the application score; (3) the affordability assessment under the Tijdelijke regeling hypothecair krediet (Trhk) and the Bank's credit risk appetite; and (4) the collateral assessment. The creditworthiness assessment relies primarily on the applicant's ability to meet the obligations from income: collateral enters only through the statutory LTV limit and one scorecard characteristic, and the decision cannot be based on the property value exceeding the loan or on expected house price increases. The scorecard characteristics and the affordability assessment together take account of the factors relevant to the prospect of the applicant meeting the obligations: income level and stability, employment, existing commitments and repayment behaviour in BKR, own funds, and the nature, maturity and interest rate fixation of the loan. No acceptance decision is taken without a valid score and score band produced by the approved scorecard. Segmentation: a single scorecard is estimated for all applications; separate scorecards for starters and movers were tested and did not improve the Gini by more than one percentage point.

sections.heading: Decision-making powers and automated decisions
sections.text: The decision-making powers are defined per outcome: the decision engine recommends accept, refer or decline; an accept recommendation leads to an offer after an underwriter's file check; referrals are decided by senior underwriters within their delegated authority; decline recommendations are reviewed by an underwriter before the decision is communicated; loans above EUR 1 million or LTV above 90% for self-employed applicants are decided by Retail Credit Risk. The automated process operates only for retail mortgages and within the policy rules, cut-offs and affordability parameters approved under CR-STD-120; the automated decision process for MAS v3.0 will be submitted to the Retail Credit Committee on 2 June 2027. The framework includes control mechanisms and escalation for the automated model: quantitative limits (cut-off, referral band, affordability limits), qualitative underwriting assessment of referrals and overrides within a closed list of reasons. All decision-engine parameters (policy rules, scorecard points, cut-offs, affordability parameters) are version-controlled and changed only through the RCC approval process and model change management.

sections.heading: Affordability component
sections.text: An affordability assessment is performed for every application, taking into account verified income, existing credit commitments (BKR registrations counted at 2% of the credit limit per month, student loans, alimony, ground lease), other fixed expenses and living expenses through the Trhk financing-cost tables, which are based on Nibud reference budgets reflecting household composition. Acceptance applies the loan-to-value limit of 100% of the market value set by the Trhk (with the statutory allowances for energy-saving measures), the maximum housing cost ratio (debt-service-to-income) from the Trhk financing-cost tables, and the Bank's risk appetite limit of 6.0 times gross household income for non-NHG loans. For interest rates fixed for less than ten years, debt service is calculated at the test rate of 5.0% published under the Trhk for 2027, or the contract rate if higher. Statutory affordability limits are never overridden; the use of a statutory exception (for example refinancing without increase, or temporarily higher costs for applicants reaching state pension age within ten years) is documented with the justification required by the Trhk. Expected income increases are not taken into account unless supported by documented evidence permitted under the Trhk, such as a written salary increase in the employment contract. The criteria are designed so that credit is granted only where the obligations are likely to be met without undue hardship or over-indebtedness for the household.

sections.heading: Collateral component and valuation
sections.text: Residential property is valued for every application using reliable valuation standards: a full valuation by an NRVT-registered valuer validated by NWWI, or, within the NHG conditions, a model-based desktop valuation. A desktop valuation is accepted only when the valuation model reports a high confidence level (forecast standard deviation of at most 10%) and the LTV is at most 90%; otherwise the underwriter requires a full valuation, and the valuer remains responsible for the value. The desktop valuation model is a vendor model operating at postcode and property-type level, backtested quarterly by the vendor against Kadaster transaction prices (median absolute error 6.8% in 2026) and reviewed annually by Collateral Management. The Bank remains responsible for the appropriateness of the valuation model; its methodology and assumptions are documented in the collateral valuation policy, which is outside the scope of this MDD. The LTV characteristic in the scorecard uses the value used for the statutory LTV test.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The scorecard is developed on the frozen reference data set RDS-MAS-3.0-F1, documented in the approved RDS documentation EVD-18-RDS version 1.0. The development sample consists of applications from January 2019 to September 2023, split randomly into an estimation sample (80%: 137,840 disbursed loans, 606 bads) and an out-of-sample hold-out (20%: 34,460 loans, 152 bads); the out-of-time sample consists of applications from October 2023 to September 2024 (38,100 loans, 168 bads). The samples were fixed on 23 April 2027, before estimation, and the out-of-time sample was not used for variable selection, coarse classing or estimation. Declined applications (62,300) are used only for reject inference (section 4.4). Data deficiencies DD-18-01 to DD-18-03 are described in RDS section 6.2.

sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three approaches were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements including explainability to applicants, data, out-of-time Gini, stability, interpretability and implementation in the decision engine): (a) a logistic regression scorecard with coarse-classed characteristics and weight-of-evidence transformation, (b) a gradient boosting model (LightGBM) with monotonic constraints, and (c) recalibration of MAS v2.1. Out-of-time Gini: (a) 0.61, (b) 0.63, (c) 0.55. The logistic regression scorecard was selected: the gradient boosting model is only two percentage points better, within the confidence interval of ±0.05 given 168 out-of-time bads, while the scorecard is fully transparent, produces additive points that can be explained to applicants and underwriters, and can be implemented as a points table in the decision engine. Recalibration of v2.1 was rejected because it cannot use the verified income characteristics.

sections.heading: Variable selection
sections.text: The 54 candidate characteristics were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the point of decision in the decision engine, and stability over time (PSI between application years below 0.10 or explained). Selection steps on the estimation sample: (1) coarse classing into at most six classes with monotonic bad rates where economically expected; (2) univariate analysis with information value (minimum 0.02) and univariate Gini; (3) removal of one of each pair with Spearman correlation above 0.6 or variance inflation factor above 2.5; (4) stepwise selection with significance level 1% and five-fold cross-validated Gini, followed by expert review of sign and magnitude. Every final characteristic has points consistent with economic intuition, and no characteristic has a p-value above 0.01. The 13 selected characteristics are: LTV band, housing cost ratio utilisation, employment type, months in current employment, BKR negative registration in last five years, number of active BKR consumer credits, BKR credit limit utilisation, own-funds contribution, NHG, loan purpose, fixed-rate period, relationship with the Bank (current account with salary credit for 24 months or more) and number of applicants.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and score scaling
sections.text: The scorecard is estimated as a logistic regression of the bad flag on the weight-of-evidence values of the 13 characteristics, on the reject-inference-augmented estimation sample with case weights. Score scaling: base score 600 at good:bad odds of 50:1 and 20 points to double the odds; points per attribute are rounded to integers, and the score range is 480 to 720. The largest point ranges are housing cost ratio utilisation (58 points between the lowest and highest class), BKR negative registration (52 points), LTV band (41 points) and employment type (33 points). The model optimises the log-likelihood of the bad outcome, so the score orders applicants by the estimated probability of early payment problems; the coefficients of the weight-of-evidence variables range from 0.71 to 1.12, indicating no material over- or under-weighting relative to univariate evidence.

sections.heading: Reject inference
sections.text: Because the known outcomes cover only accepted and disbursed applications, reject inference is performed on the 62,300 declined applications. The selected method is fuzzy augmentation: each declined application is included twice, as good and as bad, weighted by its inferred bad probability from the known good/bad model, multiplied by a factor k = 2.6 that reflects the higher risk of declined applicants. The assumption that declined applicants are riskier than accepted applicants with the same score is supported by the external performance of the 11,300 declined applicants who obtained consumer credit elsewhere: their BKR arrears rate within 24 months is 6.9% against 2.7% for accepted applicants with comparable scores and new consumer credit, a ratio of 2.6 used as k. Sensitivity to the reject inference method was assessed with hard-cut-off augmentation, parcelling and no reject inference: out-of-time Gini varies between 0.60 and 0.62, the expected bad rate per score band changes by at most 0.09 percentage points, and the approval rate at the proposed cut-off changes by at most 0.6 percentage points. Applications declined by statutory affordability limits (41,900) are included in the inference, because the scorecard is applied only after these limits in production, but their weight is capped to prevent the affordability decline population from dominating.

sections.heading: Economic rationale of characteristics
sections.text: All final characteristics have a direction consistent with credit experience: higher LTV, higher utilisation of the maximum housing cost, temporary employment, short employment duration, negative BKR history, more active consumer credits and higher limit utilisation increase risk; own funds, NHG, a longer fixed-rate period, an existing salary relationship and two applicants reduce risk. The key design choices and their rationale are documented: a points-based additive scorecard to ensure explainability, reject inference to address selection bias, the exclusion of age and other protected attributes, and the restriction of collateral to one characteristic so that the assessment remains primarily income-based. The housing cost ratio utilisation captures the margin between actual and maximum permitted housing costs and is the strongest characteristic, which is expected in the Dutch framework where the statutory maximum is binding for about a quarter of starters.

sections.heading: Calibration of expected bad rates
sections.text: The scorecard is calibrated to the long-run bad rate of the development period (0.44%) by an intercept adjustment on the estimation sample, and the expected bad rate per score band is derived from the scaling (odds doubling every 20 points). Eight score bands are defined for monitoring and cut-off setting, from band 1 (below 575, expected bad rate 3.9%) to band 8 (680 and above, 0.07%). On the out-of-time sample, observed bad rates are within the 95% Jeffreys interval of the expected rate for all eight bands, and the portfolio expected bad rate of 0.46% compares with an observed 0.44%. The expected bad rates are used for cut-off setting and front-end monitoring; they are not used as PD estimates for capital or provisioning.

sections.heading: Cut-offs and referral band
sections.text: The cut-off is based on the expected bad rate per score band, the target approval rate and the risk-adjusted return within the credit risk appetite: applications with a score of 600 or above are accepted (subject to the other components), 575–599 are referred for manual underwriting and below 575 are declined, which corresponds to a marginal bad rate of 2.0% at the accept cut-off where the risk-adjusted return of the marginal loan becomes negative. The proposal documents an expected overall approval rate of 81.6% (current 80.9%), an expected bad rate of the accepted population of 0.37% (current 0.41%), an expected loss of 0.04% of new production, and a swap-set analysis against the current cut-off: 1,420 applications per year newly accepted (expected bad rate 1.1%) and 1,610 newly declined (2.6%). They are reviewed at least annually and after any material change in the applicant population, the scorecard or the credit risk appetite. The full proposal is in EVD-18-CUT.

sections.heading: Stability
sections.text: Stability was assessed across application years and segments. The Gini per application year ranges from 0.58 (2020) to 0.65 (2022). The PSI of the score between the estimation sample and the out-of-time sample is 0.06, and between the estimation sample and applications from October 2025 to March 2026 0.09. Bootstrap resampling of the estimation sample (1,000 replications) gives a standard deviation of the points per attribute of at most 3 points, and no characteristic changes sign in any replication. The score band distribution is stable, with a maximum change of 1.4 percentage points in any band between 2023 and 2025 applications.

sections.heading: Challenger comparison and benchmarking
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, MAS v3.0 was compared with a challenger model, the gradient boosting model of section 4.1 (out-of-time Gini 0.63), and with the current model MAS v2.1 as benchmark (0.53). The challenger outperforms the scorecard by two Gini points, which is within the statistical uncertainty; the difference is explained by interactions between LTV and housing cost utilisation that the additive scorecard does not capture. The scorecard is retained because of its transparency and explainability to applicants, and the interaction is monitored through the observed-to-expected bad rate in the high-LTV, high-utilisation segment. Against v2.1, 64% of the Gini improvement comes from the verified income characteristics and the housing cost ratio utilisation.

sections.heading: Sensitivity analysis
sections.text: Sensitivity analyses cover the key assumptions, parameters and input data: the target definition (strict default flag, 18- and 36-month windows), the treatment of indeterminates (as good), the reject inference method and factor k (1.5 to 4.0), the exclusions, the coarse classing boundaries, the calibration window and the expert judgements. The out-of-time Gini ranges from 0.59 to 0.62 across these alternatives, and the approval rate at the proposed cut-off from 80.9% to 82.1%. The effect of the material expert judgements (EJ-18-01 bad flag, EJ-18-04 reject inference factor, EJ-18-05 coarse classing of employment duration) was quantified with these sensitivity analyses, with Gini impacts of at most 0.4 percentage points. A stress sensitivity of the affordability component shows that at a test rate of 6.0% instead of 5.0% the approval rate falls by 3.8 percentage points, and a 10% income reduction would bring 7% of accepted applicants above the maximum housing cost ratio.

sections.heading: Explainability and reason codes

sections.heading: Robustness, cybersecurity and resilience
sections.text: The scorecard performs consistently: points are fixed after approval, perturbation of continuous inputs by ±5% changes the score band for 3.2% of applications and the recommendation for 0.9%, and missing or invalid inputs are routed to referral. The scorecard does not learn after deployment; new versions are estimated offline and approved as model changes, so outputs cannot feed back into the model during use, and the feedback loop through future training data is addressed by reject inference. Resilience against manipulation is ensured by verification of inputs against independent documents, restricted access to the points table in the decision engine, integrity checks of the parameter release and logging; attempts to game the application (for example repeated submissions with altered income) are detected by the application fraud rules.

sections.heading: Human oversight and overrides
sections.text: The decision process is designed for effective human oversight: underwriters see the score, score band, reason codes, policy rule results and affordability outcome in the underwriting screen, can disregard or override the recommendation within their authority, and Retail Credit Risk can suspend automated recommendations and route all applications to manual underwriting through a decision-engine switch. Underwriters are trained on the capacities and limitations of the scorecard, including the segments with lower accuracy, and monitoring dashboards show score distributions and override rates so that anomalies are detected. To counter automation bias, the underwriting manual requires an independent assessment of the credit file for every referral and decline, and a quarterly quality review samples 100 accepted applications for file quality independently of the score. Oversight is assigned to underwriters with delegated authority granted by the RCC, completed training and the support of Retail Credit Risk. Low-side and high-side overrides may be applied only by underwriters with delegated authority, using one of 12 reason codes from a closed list and a written rationale; overrides are permitted only on relevant information not captured by the scorecard; each override records the reason code, rationale, evidence, proposer and an approver in Credit Risk Management independent of the proposer. Non-overridable rules (active default, fraud indicators, statutory affordability limits) cannot be overridden in the decision engine. Override reasons do not relate to protected attributes, and override decisions are included in outcome testing.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan and KPIs
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-MAS-3.0 is part of this chapter; it was approved by the Model Owner on 9 June 2027 and is submitted for review by Model Validation before go-live. It defines each KPI with calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments and responsible person, covering discriminatory power, calibration, population and characteristic stability, production data quality, overrides, policy rule hit rates and model coverage. Front-end monitoring is performed monthly (application volumes, approval rates, score PSI, characteristic PSI, policy rule hit rates, override rates); back-end monitoring quarterly once outcomes are available (Gini, observed versus expected bad rates per score band, vintage curves, early delinquency at 6 and 12 months on book). PSI of the score and of each characteristic is computed against the development sample with green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25 and red above 0.25. The Gini is compared with development, with a relative decline above 10% amber and above 20% red, and a Gini below 0.50 is red regardless of the change. Observed bad rates are compared with expected bad rates per score band and for the portfolio using the Jeffreys test of MV-HB-003. KPIs are computed for the whole model and per score band, loan purpose, NHG and employment type. This plan is also the post-market monitoring plan of the high-risk AI system: it actively collects and analyses performance data throughout the lifetime of the system.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: Formal monitoring reports are produced quarterly, in line with the minimum frequency for Tier 1 models, and finalised within 60 calendar days after the reference period. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner with its cause documented; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use, and changes follow MRM-STD-050. sections.text: Override rates are monitored monthly per product and direction; a rate above 5% of decisions triggers an analysis by the Model Owner and reporting to the Retail Credit Committee and to Model Risk Management. sections.heading: Purpose, scope and intended use
sections.text: Cover block: document title "Acceptance scorecard development document"; model MDL-18 (Mortgage Acceptance Scorecard), model version 3.0; document version 1.0; status Approved (submitted for gate G1); author L. Mulder; reviewer K. de Vries; approvers E. Visser (Director Retail Credit Risk, Model Owner) and P. Jansen (Head of Retail Credit Risk Modelling); approval date 9 June 2027. MAS v3.0 is a logistic regression application scorecard that ranks new Dutch residential mortgage applications of natural persons by the probability of becoming 90 days past due or defaulted within 24 months, expressed as a score between 480 and 720. Together with the policy rules, the affordability assessment and the collateral assessment it produces an accept, refer or decline recommendation in the mortgage decision engine. The scorecard forms part of the thorough creditworthiness assessment that the Bank performs before concluding every mortgage credit agreement. Intended users are the Bank's mortgage underwriters (acceptants), Retail Credit Risk (cut-off and policy management) and the Retail Credit Committee. The expected bad rate per score band is used as secondary input to risk-based pricing analysis; the score is not used for IRB, provisioning or behavioural purposes. Regulatory use: credit origination. The model is Tier 1. MAS v3.0 will be used in credit decisions only after approval following independent validation, and only within its approved scope of application.

sections.heading: AI system assessment and AI Act classification
sections.text: The scorecard was assessed against the AI system definition of Art. 3(1) AI Act. Its coefficients and score bands are inferred from historical data by statistical estimation rather than set by humans, and it generates predictions that influence decisions on natural persons; although logistic regression is an established statistical technique, the Bank concluded, conservatively and in agreement with the AI Governance Office (review AIGO-2026-118 of 18 November 2026), that MAS v3.0 qualifies as an AI system. Because it is intended to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons, MAS v3.0 is classified as a high-risk AI system under Art. 6(2) and Annex III point 5(b) and is registered as such in the model inventory and the AI Inventory (AIUC-2026-041); it is not used for fraud detection. The Art. 6(3) derogation is not relied upon, because the system performs profiling of natural persons. The AI Act classification was recorded in the model inventory before gate G1. The Bank acts as provider (it develops the system and puts it into service under its own name) and as deployer. The high-risk requirements apply from 2 December 2027; MAS v3.0 is planned to be put into service on 17 January 2028, after the conformity assessment described in the AI Act technical documentation EVD-18-FRIA.

sections.heading: Model design and decision framework
sections.text: Each acceptance decision combines four components, all of which must be passed unless an authorised override applies: (1) policy rules (for example an active BKR default registration, an application fraud indicator, ineligible property type); (2) the application score; (3) the affordability assessment under the Tijdelijke regeling hypothecair krediet (Trhk) and the Bank's credit risk appetite; and (4) the collateral assessment. The creditworthiness assessment relies primarily on the applicant's ability to meet the obligations from income: collateral enters only through the statutory LTV limit and one scorecard characteristic, and the decision cannot be based on the property value exceeding the loan or on expected house price increases. The scorecard characteristics and the affordability assessment together take account of the factors relevant to the prospect of the applicant meeting the obligations: income level and stability, employment, existing commitments and repayment behaviour in BKR, own funds, and the nature, maturity and interest rate fixation of the loan. No acceptance decision is taken without a valid score and score band produced by the approved scorecard. Segmentation: a single scorecard is estimated for all applications; separate scorecards for starters and movers were tested and did not improve the Gini by more than one percentage point.

sections.heading: Decision-making powers and automated decisions
sections.text: The decision-making powers are defined per outcome: the decision engine recommends accept, refer or decline; an accept recommendation leads to an offer after an underwriter's file check; referrals are decided by senior underwriters within their delegated authority; decline recommendations are reviewed by an underwriter before the decision is communicated; loans above EUR 1 million or LTV above 90% for self-employed applicants are decided by Retail Credit Risk. sections.heading: Affordability component
sections.text: An affordability assessment is performed for every application, taking into account verified income, existing credit commitments (BKR registrations counted at 2% of the credit limit per month, student loans, alimony, ground lease), other fixed expenses and living expenses through the Trhk financing-cost tables, which are based on Nibud reference budgets reflecting household composition. Acceptance applies the loan-to-value limit of 100% of the market value set by the Trhk (with the statutory allowances for energy-saving measures), the maximum housing cost ratio (debt-service-to-income) from the Trhk financing-cost tables, and the Bank's risk appetite limit of 6.0 times gross household income for non-NHG loans. For interest rates fixed for less than ten years, debt service is calculated at the test rate of 5.0% published under the Trhk for 2027, or the contract rate if higher. Statutory affordability limits are never overridden; the use of a statutory exception (for example refinancing without increase, or temporarily higher costs for applicants reaching state pension age within ten years) is documented with the justification required by the Trhk. Expected income increases are not taken into account unless supported by documented evidence permitted under the Trhk, such as a written salary increase in the employment contract. The criteria are designed so that credit is granted only where the obligations are likely to be met without undue hardship or over-indebtedness for the household.

sections.heading: Collateral component and valuation
sections.text: Residential property is valued for every application using reliable valuation standards: a full valuation by an NRVT-registered valuer validated by NWWI, or, within the NHG conditions, a model-based desktop valuation. A desktop valuation is accepted only when the valuation model reports a high confidence level (forecast standard deviation of at most 10%) and the LTV is at most 90%; otherwise the underwriter requires a full valuation, and the valuer remains responsible for the value. The desktop valuation model is a vendor model operating at postcode and property-type level, backtested quarterly by the vendor against Kadaster transaction prices (median absolute error 6.8% in 2026) and reviewed annually by Collateral Management. The Bank remains responsible for the appropriateness of the valuation model; its methodology and assumptions are documented in the collateral valuation policy, which is outside the scope of this MDD. The LTV characteristic in the scorecard uses the value used for the statutory LTV test.

sections.heading: Data
sections.text: The scorecard is developed on the frozen reference data set RDS-MAS-3.0-F1, documented in the approved RDS documentation EVD-18-RDS version 1.0. sections.heading: Alternatives considered and selection
sections.text: Three approaches were assessed against documented criteria (regulatory requirements including explainability to applicants, data, out-of-time Gini, stability, interpretability and implementation in the decision engine): (a) a logistic regression scorecard with coarse-classed characteristics and weight-of-evidence transformation, (b) a gradient boosting model (LightGBM) with monotonic constraints, and (c) recalibration of MAS v2.1. Out-of-time Gini: (a) 0.61, (b) 0.63, (c) 0.55. The logistic regression scorecard was selected: the gradient boosting model is only two percentage points better, within the confidence interval of ±0.05 given 168 out-of-time bads, while the scorecard is fully transparent, produces additive points that can be explained to applicants and underwriters, and can be implemented as a points table in the decision engine. Recalibration of v2.1 was rejected because it cannot use the verified income characteristics.

sections.heading: Variable selection
sections.text: The 54 candidate characteristics were assessed for economic rationale, availability at the point of decision in the decision engine, and stability over time (PSI between application years below 0.10 or explained). Selection steps on the estimation sample: (1) coarse classing into at most six classes with monotonic bad rates where economically expected; (2) univariate analysis with information value (minimum 0.02) and univariate Gini; (3) removal of one of each pair with Spearman correlation above 0.6 or variance inflation factor above 2.5; (4) stepwise selection with significance level 1% and five-fold cross-validated Gini, followed by expert review of sign and magnitude. Every final characteristic has points consistent with economic intuition, and no characteristic has a p-value above 0.01. The 13 selected characteristics are: LTV band, housing cost ratio utilisation, employment type, months in current employment, BKR negative registration in last five years, number of active BKR consumer credits, BKR credit limit utilisation, own-funds contribution, NHG, loan purpose, fixed-rate period, relationship with the Bank (current account with salary credit for 24 months or more) and number of applicants.

sections.heading: Estimation technique and score scaling
sections.text: The scorecard is estimated as a logistic regression of the bad flag on the weight-of-evidence values of the 13 characteristics, on the reject-inference-augmented estimation sample with case weights. Score scaling: base score 600 at good:bad odds of 50:1 and 20 points to double the odds; points per attribute are rounded to integers, and the score range is 480 to 720. The largest point ranges are housing cost ratio utilisation (58 points between the lowest and highest class), BKR negative registration (52 points), LTV band (41 points) and employment type (33 points). The model optimises the log-likelihood of the bad outcome, so the score orders applicants by the estimated probability of early payment problems; the coefficients of the weight-of-evidence variables range from 0.71 to 1.12, indicating no material over- or under-weighting relative to univariate evidence.

sections.heading: Reject inference
sections.text: Because the known outcomes cover only accepted and disbursed applications, reject inference is performed on the 62,300 declined applications. The selected method is fuzzy augmentation: each declined application is included twice, as good and as bad, weighted by its inferred bad probability from the known good/bad model, multiplied by a factor k = 2.6 that reflects the higher risk of declined applicants. The assumption that declined applicants are riskier than accepted applicants with the same score is supported by the external performance of the 11,300 declined applicants who obtained consumer credit elsewhere: their BKR arrears rate within 24 months is 6.9% against 2.7% for accepted applicants with comparable scores and new consumer credit, a ratio of 2.6 used as k. Sensitivity to the reject inference method was assessed with hard-cut-off augmentation, parcelling and no reject inference: out-of-time Gini varies between 0.60 and 0.62, the expected bad rate per score band changes by at most 0.09 percentage points, and the approval rate at the proposed cut-off changes by at most 0.6 percentage points. Applications declined by statutory affordability limits (41,900) are included in the inference, because the scorecard is applied only after these limits in production, but their weight is capped to prevent the affordability decline population from dominating.

sections.heading: Economic rationale of characteristics
sections.text: All final characteristics have a direction consistent with credit experience: higher LTV, higher utilisation of the maximum housing cost, temporary employment, short employment duration, negative BKR history, more active consumer credits and higher limit utilisation increase risk; own funds, NHG, a longer fixed-rate period, an existing salary relationship and two applicants reduce risk. The key design choices and their rationale are documented: a points-based additive scorecard to ensure explainability, reject inference to address selection bias, the exclusion of age and other protected attributes, and the restriction of collateral to one characteristic so that the assessment remains primarily income-based. The housing cost ratio utilisation captures the margin between actual and maximum permitted housing costs and is the strongest characteristic, which is expected in the Dutch framework where the statutory maximum is binding for about a quarter of starters.

sections.heading: Calibration of expected bad rates
sections.text: The scorecard is calibrated to the long-run bad rate of the development period (0.44%) by an intercept adjustment on the estimation sample, and the expected bad rate per score band is derived from the scaling (odds doubling every 20 points). Eight score bands are defined for monitoring and cut-off setting, from band 1 (below 575, expected bad rate 3.9%) to band 8 (680 and above, 0.07%). On the out-of-time sample, observed bad rates are within the 95% Jeffreys interval of the expected rate for all eight bands, and the portfolio expected bad rate of 0.46% compares with an observed 0.44%. The expected bad rates are used for cut-off setting and front-end monitoring; they are not used as PD estimates for capital or provisioning.

sections.heading: Cut-offs and referral band
sections.text: The cut-off is based on the expected bad rate per score band, the target approval rate and the risk-adjusted return within the credit risk appetite: applications with a score of 600 or above are accepted (subject to the other components), 575–599 are referred for manual underwriting and below 575 are declined, which corresponds to a marginal bad rate of 2.0% at the accept cut-off where the risk-adjusted return of the marginal loan becomes negative. The proposal documents an expected overall approval rate of 81.6% (current 80.9%), an expected bad rate of the accepted population of 0.37% (current 0.41%), an expected loss of 0.04% of new production, and a swap-set analysis against the current cut-off: 1,420 applications per year newly accepted (expected bad rate 1.1%) and 1,610 newly declined (2.6%). The cut-off and referral band were approved by the Retail Credit Committee on 2 June 2027 (RCC-2027-11), effective upon model approval, before implementation. They are reviewed at least annually and after any material change in the applicant population, the scorecard or the credit risk appetite. The full proposal is in EVD-18-CUT.

sections.heading: Challenger comparison and benchmarking
sections.text: As a Tier 1 model, MAS v3.0 was compared with a challenger model, the gradient boosting model of section 4.1 (out-of-time Gini 0.63), and with the current model MAS v2.1 as benchmark (0.53). The scorecard is retained because of its transparency and explainability to applicants, and the interaction is monitored through the observed-to-expected bad rate in the high-LTV, high-utilisation segment. Against v2.1, 64% of the Gini improvement comes from the verified income characteristics and the housing cost ratio utilisation.

sections.heading: Robustness, cybersecurity and resilience
sections.text: The scorecard performs consistently: points are fixed after approval, perturbation of continuous inputs by ±5% changes the score band for 3.2% of applications and the recommendation for 0.9%, and missing or invalid inputs are routed to referral. The scorecard does not learn after deployment; new versions are estimated offline and approved as model changes, so outputs cannot feed back into the model during use, and the feedback loop through future training data is addressed by reject inference. Resilience against manipulation is ensured by verification of inputs against independent documents, restricted access to the points table in the decision engine, integrity checks of the parameter release and logging; attempts to game the application (for example repeated submissions with altered income) are detected by the application fraud rules.

sections.heading: Human oversight and overrides
sections.text: The decision process is designed for effective human oversight: underwriters see the score, score band, reason codes, policy rule results and affordability outcome in the underwriting screen, can disregard or override the recommendation within their authority, and Retail Credit Risk can suspend automated recommendations and route all applications to manual underwriting through a decision-engine switch. Underwriters are trained on the capacities and limitations of the scorecard, including the segments with lower accuracy, and monitoring dashboards show score distributions and override rates so that anomalies are detected. To counter automation bias, the underwriting manual requires an independent assessment of the credit file for every referral and decline, and a quarterly quality review samples 100 accepted applications for file quality independently of the score. Oversight is assigned to underwriters with delegated authority granted by the RCC, completed training and the support of Retail Credit Risk. Low-side and high-side overrides may be applied only by underwriters with delegated authority, using one of 12 reason codes from a closed list and a written rationale; overrides are permitted only on relevant information not captured by the scorecard; each override records the reason code, rationale, evidence, proposer and an approver in Credit Risk Management independent of the proposer. Non-overridable rules (active default, fraud indicators, statutory affordability limits) cannot be overridden in the decision engine. Override reasons do not relate to protected attributes, and override decisions are included in outcome testing.

sections.heading: Monitoring plan and KPIs
sections.text: The monitoring plan MP-MAS-3.0 is part of this chapter; it was approved by the Model Owner on 9 June 2027 and is submitted for review by Model Validation before go-live. It defines each KPI with calculation, amber and red thresholds, frequency, data and reference period, segments and responsible person, covering discriminatory power, calibration, population and characteristic stability, production data quality, overrides, policy rule hit rates and model coverage. Front-end monitoring is performed monthly (application volumes, approval rates, score PSI, characteristic PSI, policy rule hit rates, override rates); back-end monitoring quarterly once outcomes are available (Gini, observed versus expected bad rates per score band, vintage curves, early delinquency at 6 and 12 months on book). PSI of the score and of each characteristic is computed against the development sample with green below 0.10, amber 0.10–0.25 and red above 0.25. The Gini is compared with development, with a relative decline above 10% amber and above 20% red, and a Gini below 0.50 is red regardless of the change. Observed bad rates are compared with expected bad rates per score band and for the portfolio using the Jeffreys test of MV-HB-003. KPIs are computed for the whole model and per score band, loan purpose, NHG and employment type. This plan is also the post-market monitoring plan of the high-risk AI system: it actively collects and analyses performance data throughout the lifetime of the system.

sections.heading: Frequency, reporting and escalation
sections.text: Formal monitoring reports are produced quarterly, in line with the minimum frequency for Tier 1 models, and finalised within 60 calendar days after the reference period. Each amber result is analysed by the Model Owner with its cause documented; a red result, or amber on the same KPI in two consecutive cycles, is notified to Model Risk Management and Model Validation within ten business days, followed by a root cause analysis and action plan within 60 calendar days. The action plan proposes no action with justification, a temporary overlay, recalibration, redevelopment or restriction of use, and changes follow MRM-STD-050. Red results and triggers unresolved after six months are reported to the Model Risk Committee, and a red outcome requires a remediation plan approved by the Retail Credit Committee within three months. Credit Risk Management receives all monitoring reports. Where monitoring indicates that the system may present a risk to the health, safety or fundamental rights of applicants, the Model Owner suspends automated recommendations and informs the AI Governance Office, which decides on notification of the market surveillance authority. The plan is updated at every model change and reviewed annually; monitoring code (repository rcrm-mas-monitoring) and data are version controlled so that results are reproducible.

Each report lists overlays in place and shows model coverage: the share of applications scored and applications decided without a valid score. sections.heading: Early warning indicators
sections.text: The scorecard contributes to early warning at portfolio and segment level: the monthly front-end report and the quarterly back-end report include early delinquency (30 days past due at 6 and 12 months on book) per score band, vintage and segment, which are early warning indicators for the mortgage origination portfolio. sections.heading: Risk management system
sections.text: A risk management system is established for MAS v3.0 as a continuous iterative process integrated into the model lifecycle of MRM-POL-001: risks are identified at the development plan, reassessed at gate G1, at validation, before go-live and at every quarterly monitoring cycle, and the risk register RR-MAS-3.0 is reviewed at least annually and at every model change. The register identifies and evaluates known and reasonably foreseeable risks to fundamental rights under the intended purpose and foreseeable misuse: unjustified decline or over-crediting through inaccurate scores, indirect discrimination by nationality or age through proxies, automation bias of underwriters, use of the score outside its scope (for example for further advances or pricing without validation), manipulation of application data, and opacity towards applicants. Targeted measures are adopted for each risk: validation and monitoring of accuracy, proxy screening and outcome testing, training and file review against automation bias, technical scope restriction in the decision engine, independent verification of inputs, and reason codes with a right to human review. The residual risk of each hazard and the overall residual risk were judged acceptable by the Use Case Owner and the AI Governance Office on 4 June 2027, with the non-EU approval-rate disparity rated medium residual risk under monitoring.

documents.title: Cut-off, affordability and override proposal – Retail Credit Committee paper

sections.heading: Purpose of the proposal
sections.text: This paper to the Retail Credit Committee (RCC) of 2 June 2027 proposes the cut-off, referral band, affordability parameters and override policy for the Mortgage Acceptance Scorecard v3.0 (MDL-18), and requests approval of the automated decision process, effective upon approval of the model by the Model Risk Committee. It was prepared by Retail Credit Risk and Retail Credit Risk Modelling and is sponsored by the Model Owner E. Visser. The analyses are based on the out-of-time sample and on 29,400 applications of October 2025 – March 2026 (the recent applicant population), scored with MAS v3.0 in the development environment.

sections.heading: Decision framework
sections.text: Each application must pass the policy rules, the score, the affordability assessment and the collateral assessment; an application is accepted only if all four are passed or an authorised override applies. The credit-granting criteria are designed to avoid undue hardship and over-indebtedness: the score cut-off applies in addition to, and never instead of, the statutory affordability limits. The proposal does not change the policy rules, which were reviewed by the RCC in December 2026.
