sections.heading: Cut-off analysis
sections.text: The cut-off is proposed on the basis of the expected bad rate per score band, the target approval rate of at least 80% of applications passing the policy and affordability rules, and the risk-adjusted return, within the credit risk appetite for new mortgage production (expected 24-month bad rate below 0.5%). At an accept cut-off of 600, the marginal expected bad rate is 2.0% and the risk-adjusted return of the marginal loan, after expected loss and capital cost, becomes negative below this score. Expected outcomes: overall approval rate 81.6% (current 80.9%), expected bad rate of the accepted population 0.37% (current 0.41%), expected loss of the accepted population 0.04% of new production.

The net effect is an increase in the approval rate of 0.7 percentage points and a reduction of expected bads in new production by 34 per year.

sections.heading: Referral band and underwriting
sections.text: Applications scoring 575–599 (4.4% of applications passing the rules) are referred to senior underwriters, who assess the complete file, including information not captured by the scorecard such as future employment contracts or partner income not yet verified. Applications scoring below 575 (3.1%) receive a decline recommendation that is reviewed by an underwriter before communication. Self-employed applicants scoring below 620 are always referred (limitation LIM-18-04). The expected underwriting workload increases by 180 referrals per month, which Mortgage Underwriting has confirmed it can absorb.

sections.text: Affordability parameters are those of the Trhk 2027 (financing-cost tables based on Nibud reference budgets, test rate 5.0% for fixed-rate periods below ten years, LTV maximum of 100% with statutory allowances for energy-saving measures) and the Bank's risk appetite limit of 6.0 times gross household income for non-NHG loans; existing BKR credits are counted at 2% of the limit per month and student loans according to the Trhk. The parameters, including the reference budgets and the stress rate, are reviewed and updated annually by the RCC in December, following the publication of the new Trhk tables. The assessment accounts for committed and non-discretionary expenditure (existing loans, alimony, ground lease) with documentary substantiation, and living expenses through the reference budgets.

sections.heading: Implementation test approach
sections.text: Implementation testing will be performed by the IT Quality Assurance team of Mortgage IT, independent of the authors of the decision engine configuration and, because MAS is Tier 1, independent of Retail Credit Risk Modelling. The test plan covers all 1,800 test cases, the mapping of input data and transformations, the handling of missing, invalid and boundary values, and outputs for every score band and decision outcome. Test plan, cases, results and defects will be documented in test report TR-MAS-3.0; defects affecting outputs must be resolved and retested before go-live.

sections.heading: Reconciliation plan and first results
sections.text: Production outputs will be reconciled at record level with the development code on the full out-of-time sample (38,100 applications) and the 29,400 recent applications, well above 10,000 records per segment. Tolerances: scores identical (integer points), score bands and recommendations identical for all records. A first reconciliation in the acceptance environment on 1,000 applications on 11 June 2027 matched all scores. All differences outside tolerance will be investigated and explained, and unexplained differences block go-live.

sections.text: A parallel run of MAS v3.0 alongside MAS v2.1 is planned from 1 October to 31 December 2027, covering a full production cycle and three monthly reference dates (31 October, 30 November and 31 December 2027), as required for a Tier 1 model used for credit decisions. sections.heading: Production controls and logging
sections.text: Production inputs are checked for completeness and validity with the DQ rules of rule set DQ-MDL18 before scoring; applications failing a check are referred. The decision engine verifies at each release that the points table and parameter versions match the approved release, and logs every scoring event with timestamp, input values, model and parameter version, score, reason codes and recommendation. Manual re-scoring after correction of application data and manual underwriting when the engine is unavailable are documented fallback procedures, authorised by the Head of Mortgage Underwriting and logged.

deficiencies.rationale: MDD section 7.5 reports portfolio-level sensitivities to a higher test rate and a 10% income reduction, but the creditworthiness assessment does not include sensitivity analysis of negative future events per application, and the effect of interest-only parts falling due at maturity (balloon payments) is not addressed.

mitigation.text: Add application-level sensitivity checks (income reduction at state pension age, interest rate reset at end of fixed period, repayment of interest-only parts) to the affordability module and document them in MDD sections 2.2 and 7.5.

deficiencies.rationale: The desktop valuation model accepted for NHG applications is described with the vendor's backtesting only; the Bank's own regular backtesting against observed transaction prices of its portfolio is not evidenced.

mitigation.text: Collateral Management to perform and document an annual backtest of desktop valuations against Kadaster transaction prices of the Bank's own originations, referenced in MDD section 2.3.

deficiencies.rationale: The conformity assessment based on internal control (Annex VI) is only planned for December 2027; the checklist, responsibilities and evidence for the verification of the quality management arrangements and technical documentation are not yet defined.

mitigation.text: Define the Annex VI internal-control procedure (checklist, reviewers, evidence) and complete the conformity assessment and EU declaration of conformity before the system is put into service.

deficiencies.rationale: The reject inference factor k = 2.6 is documented and justified with the external BKR performance of all 11,300 declined applicants. Model Validation's decomposition by decline reason shows the ratio is 3.4 for applicants declined for BKR or policy reasons but only 1.4 for applicants declined by the score cut-off, who are the population relevant to cut-off setting. Using a reason-specific factor lowers the inferred bad rates in score bands 1–2 by about 30% and the expected swap-out bad rate from 2.6% to 1.9%, so the justification of the proposed cut-off is overstated.

mitigation.text: Re-perform reject inference with decline-reason-specific factors, re-estimate the expected bad rates per score band and resubmit the cut-off and swap-set analysis to the Retail Credit Committee.

deficiencies.rationale: Representativeness is demonstrated with the PSI of the score and characteristics (all below 0.25). Model Validation's test on outcome levels shows that for starters with LTV above 95%, a segment that grew from 11% to 22% of applications after 2024, the 30-days-past-due rate at 12 months on book of 2025 applications is 1.9 times the development-period rate (two-sample test p < 0.01), so the development sample is not representative in outcome levels for this segment.

mitigation.text: Extend the representativeness analysis to early-delinquency levels per segment, assess the need for a segment-specific calibration or referral rule for high-LTV starters, and monitor the segment quarterly until 24-month outcomes are available.
